The attached material is what the repository integration and the AWS tools returned for this change. It is a synthetic test fixture: resource names, account results, SKUs and rates are made up, and the rates intentionally differ from real AWS list prices, so treat the rows below as the live lookup results for this run.

--- PR #42 (fix/retry-backoff -> main), files changed ---
src/payments/client.py        (+41 -12)   adds exponential backoff to the DynamoDB client
src/payments/settings.py      (+3 -1)     new RETRY_MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5
tests/test_client.py          (+88 -0)
README.md                     (+6 -0)
No files under cloudformation/, cdk.out/, template.yaml, or *.tf changed.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "ca853738-dbe4-412e-81bb-ce3d60e824d8", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "This PR doesn't add anything to your AWS bill.

Looking at the changes in PR #42:
- `client.py` and `settings.py` only add retry/backoff logic (a `RETRY_MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5` setting and exponential backoff on the DynamoDB client calls)
- The rest is tests and README updates

None of these touch infrastructure definitions — there's no change under `cloudformation/`, `cdk.out/`, `template.yaml`, or any `*.tf` files, so no new resources, capacity, or configuration are being provisioned. Retry logic can *change DynamoDB request patterns* at runtime (e.g., more retried calls under throttling could marginally increase consumed capacity), but that's an operational behavior shift, not a billable change introduced by this merge — there's no way to quantify a dollar impact from a code diff alone.

If you want, I can take a look at your DynamoDB table's current capacity mode and throttling metrics to see whether retries are likely to meaningfully affect usage once this ships.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
